meta.title: Spotting a phishing email
meta.description: In twelve minutes, learn to spot the signs of a fraudulent email and respond without taking risks.
obj.signs: Identify the warning signs of a phishing email.
obj.react: Apply the right response to a suspicious email.
s1.title: Understanding the threat
s1.welcome.title: Welcome
s1.welcome.heading: One click is enough
s1.welcome.body: Phishing means posing as a trusted contact to obtain a password, a payment or the opening of a booby-trapped file. It is the entry point for **most cyberattacks**: attackers target people rather than machines.

s2.title: Warning signs
s2.signals.title: Five signs to check
s2.signals.intro: A single sign proves nothing. Several signs together should stop you.
s2.signal.sender.title: An almost familiar sender
s2.signal.sender.body: The display name looks familiar, but the actual address is different: one changed letter, an unusual domain, a personal address for an "official" message.
s2.signal.urgency.title: Urgency or a threat
s2.signal.urgency.body: "Your account will be suspended in 24 hours." Time pressure is there to stop you from thinking.
s2.signal.links.title: Links that don't go where they say
s2.signal.links.body: Hover over a link (or long-press on mobile) to see its real destination before opening it.
s2.signal.attachments.title: An unexpected attachment
s2.signal.attachments.body: An unknown invoice, a document "to approve": an attachment you weren't expecting may contain malware.
s2.signal.requests.title: An unusual request
s2.signal.requests.body: No legitimate service asks for your password by email. A change of bank details must always be confirmed through another channel.
s2.practice.title: Practice
s2.practice.prompt: You receive "IT Service <support@it-helpdesk-secure.net>: your mailbox is full, click here within 2 hours". Which signs do you spot?
s2.practice.a: The sender's address does not belong to your company.
s2.practice.a.fb: Correct: an internal service writes from the company domain, not from a long external domain.
s2.practice.b: The message is about your mailbox.
s2.practice.b.fb: The topic itself is not a sign: genuine messages also talk about your mailbox. Look at how the request is made instead.
s2.practice.c.fb: Correct: artificial urgency is one of the most common levers.
s3.title: Responding well
s3.react.title: Three reflexes
s3.react.intro: When in doubt, the right response is simple and risk-free.
s3.step.stop.title: Don't interact
s3.step.stop.body: Don't click any link, don't open any attachment and don't reply. If you're unsure about a real contact, reach them through a channel you already know.
s3.step.report.title: Report it
s3.step.report.body: Use your organization's report button or address. Your report also protects colleagues who received the same message.
s3.step.clicked.title: If you already clicked
s3.step.clicked.body: Don't panic, but act fast: alert IT support immediately and change the affected password from the official website. The sooner the alert, the smaller the damage.
s4.title: Assessment
s4.quiz.title: Check your knowledge
q.sender.prompt: The display name is "Finance Department", the address is finance@your-company-payment.com. What do you conclude?
q.sender.a: The message is trustworthy, since the name matches a real department.
q.sender.a.fb: Anyone can choose a display name: only the actual address counts.
q.sender.b: It's suspicious: the domain looks like the company's but isn't the right one.
q.sender.b.fb: Exactly: adding a word to the domain is a classic impersonation technique.
q.sender.c: You can't conclude anything without opening the attachment.
q.sender.c.fb: Opening the attachment is precisely the risk to avoid: the address alone is already enough to raise doubt.
q.signals.prompt: Which of these are warning signs?
q.signals.a: A request for your password by email.
q.signals.a.fb: Yes: no legitimate service asks for your password by email.
q.signals.b: A link whose real destination differs from the text shown.
q.signals.b.fb: Yes: it's the most common way to lead you to a fake site.
q.signals.c: A message from a colleague you know, with expected content.
q.signals.c.fb: No: an expected message from a known sender and address is not a sign in itself.
q.signals.d.fb: No: an expected communication is not a sign, as long as it doesn't ask for anything unusual.
q.react.prompt: You clicked a suspicious link and entered your password. What do you do first?
q.react.a: I wait to see if anything unusual happens.
q.react.a.fb: Waiting gives the attacker time: every minute counts.
q.react.b: I delete the email to remove the traces.
q.react.b.fb: Deleting the email doesn't protect the account, and deprives support of useful information.
q.react.c: I alert IT support and change my password from the official website.
q.react.c.fb: That's the right response: alert quickly and cut off the attacker's access.
s4.recap.title: Summary
s4.recap.heading: Key takeaways
s4.recap.p1: Check the sender's actual address, not just the display name.
s4.recap.p2: Urgency, misleading link, unexpected attachment, unusual request: several signs together should stop you.
s4.recap.p3: When in doubt, don't click and report it. If you clicked, alert immediately.
